title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 320: The Vertical Frontier: Elevators & Cities
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 320 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Vertical Frontier: Elevators, Steel, and Urban Stratification

Paragraph 1. Until the middle of the nineteenth century, the height of city buildings was limited by one simple biological barrier: the human knee. Even though architects already knew how to build stone towers ten storeys tall, ordinary urban buildings rarely rose above five or six floors because climbing higher stairs was physically exhausting. Top-floor attics were cheap, unwanted rooms rented to servants, poor students, and struggling artists, while wealthy families occupied the prestigious first and second floors near street life.

Paragraph 2. This old hierarchy flipped suddenly in May 1854 at the New York Crystal Palace exhibition. Standing on an open lifting platform high above a nervous crowd, inventor Elisha Graves Otis ordered an assistant to cut the main cable. Instead of crashing down, the platform dropped just a few inches before Otis's spring-powered safety brake locked onto toothed rails. Paired with the new Bessemer steel process—which replaced thick stone walls with light metal frames—the safety elevator allowed skyscrapers to climb into the clouds.

Paragraph 3. In Up: The Vertical City, urban sociologist Dr. Ronald Kroll explains how elevators turned real estate values upside down. Almost overnight, top floors transformed from miserable attics into prized luxury penthouses. High above street dust, foul smells, and loud traffic, upper apartments offered bright sunlight, fresh air, and wide views of the city, while lower floors dropped in status to commercial shops.

Paragraph 4. Kroll argues that elevators did more than save tired legs; they reshaped social life. In low-rise cities, rich and poor citizens constantly crossed paths on stairwells and sidewalks. In modern skyscraper cities, however, high-speed elevators act as private transit cabins, carrying wealthy elites straight from underground garages to cloud-level suites. By removing the physical friction of stairs, Otis's invention also separated the wealthy from everyday public city life.

groups.title: Questions 6–10
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer? Write YES, NO, or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...one simple biological barrier: the human knee."
Từ cần điền: knee.
Đoạn 2: "...Otis's spring-powered safety brake locked onto toothed rails."
Từ cần điền: brake.
Đoạn 2: "Paired with the new Bessemer steel process..."
Từ cần điền: steel.
Đoạn 3: "...fresh air, and wide views of the city..."
Từ cần điền: views.
Đoạn 4: "...straight from underground garages to cloud-level suites."
Từ cần điền: garages.

q6.text: Physical fatigue from climbing stairs prevented early city buildings from exceeding six storeys.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...rarely rose above five or six floors because climbing higher stairs was physically exhausting."
Kết luận: YES.

q7.text: Top-floor attics in pre-industrial cities were reserved exclusively for wealthy families.

steps: Đoạn 1: Tầng áp mái dành cho người hầu, sinh viên nghèo; giới giàu sống ở tầng 1 và 2.
Kết luận: NO.

q8.text: New steel-making technology helped make tall skyscrapers possible alongside elevators.

steps: Đoạn 2: Quy trình thép Bessemer thay thế tường đá dày giúp xây nhà chọc trời.
Kết luận: YES.

q9.text: Dr. Ronald Kroll lives in a low-rise apartment building in New York.

steps: Đoạn 3 & 4: Không có thông tin về nơi ở cá nhân của tác giả Kroll.
Kết luận: NOT GIVEN.

q10.text: High-speed skyscraper elevators encourage rich and poor residents to meet more frequently.

steps: Đoạn 4: Ngược lại, thang máy tốc độ cao tách biệt người giàu khỏi không gian công cộng và đời sống chung.
Kết luận: NO.
